reminder: A nil ideal is an [ideal](c:ideal) in which every element is [nilpotent](c:nilpotent-element).
definition: An [ideal](c:ideal) $I$ of a [ring](c:ring) $R$ is a nil ideal when every element $x\in I$ is a [nilpotent element](c:nilpotent-element), that is, $x^n=0$ for some $n\ge1$ that depends on $x$.
examples: In $\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z}$ the ideal $\{0,2,4,6\}$ is a nil ideal, because the cube of each element is $0$.
In $k[x_1,x_2,\dots]/(x_1,x_2^2,x_3^3,\dots)$ over a field $k$, the ideal $(x_1,x_2,\dots)$ is a nil ideal, but none of its powers is $0$.
Non-example: in $\mathbb{Z}$ the ideal $2\mathbb{Z}$ is not a nil ideal, because no power of $2$ is $0$.

steps: Let $I$ be a [nilpotent ideal](c:nilpotent-ideal), so $I^n=0$ for some $n\ge1$.
For each $x\in I$ the power $x^n$ lies in $I^n$, so $x^n=0$.
So every element of $I$ is a [nilpotent element](c:nilpotent-element), and $I$ is a nil ideal.
The nil case drops the demand that one exponent $n$ works for all elements.
links.why: It shows that a nil ideal needs one exponent for each element, while a nilpotent ideal needs one exponent for the whole ideal.

steps: A nil ideal is first of all an [ideal](c:ideal) of a ring $R$.
Add the condition that every element of the ideal is nilpotent.
An ideal that meets this condition is a nil ideal.
links.why: It shows that a nil ideal is an ideal plus one condition on its elements.

reminder: An [ideal](c:ideal) is nilpotent when some power of it is the zero ideal.
definition: An [ideal](c:ideal) $I$ of a [ring](c:ring) $R$ is nilpotent when $I^n=0$ for some [natural number](c:natural-number) $n\ge1$. Here $I^n$ is the ideal generated by all products $x_1\cdots x_n$ with $x_1,\dots,x_n\in I$.
examples: In $\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z}$ the ideal $(2)$ is nilpotent, because $(2)^3=(8)=0$.
In $k[x]/(x^3)$ over a field $k$, the ideal $(x)$ is nilpotent, because $(x)^3=0$.
In the ring of upper triangular $n\times n$ matrices, the strictly upper triangular matrices form a nilpotent ideal $I$ with $I^n=0$.
Non-example: in $\mathbb{Z}$ the ideal $2\mathbb{Z}$ is not nilpotent, because $(2\mathbb{Z})^n=2^n\mathbb{Z}\ne0$ for every $n$.

steps: Let $I$ be a nilpotent ideal with $I^n=0$.
Each $x\in I$ has $x^n\in I^n=0$.
So every element of $I$ is a [nilpotent element](c:nilpotent-element).
Hence $I$ is a [nil ideal](c:nil-ideal), and the nilpotent case adds one common exponent.
links.why: It shows that every result about nil ideals applies to nilpotent ideals.

reminder: A nilpotent space is a connected space whose [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) is nilpotent and acts nilpotently on the higher homotopy groups.
definition: A [path connected space](c:path-connected-space) $X$ is nilpotent when its [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) $\pi_1(X)$ is a [nilpotent group](c:nilpotent-group) and acts nilpotently on every [homotopy group](c:homotopy-group) $\pi_n(X)$ with $n\ge2$. A group $G$ acts nilpotently on an abelian group $A$ when $A$ has a finite chain of $G$-invariant subgroups $A=A_0\supseteq\dots\supseteq A_k=0$ with $G$ acting trivially on every quotient $A_i/A_{i+1}$.
examples: Every simply connected space is nilpotent, for example the sphere $S^n$ with $n\ge2$.
Every path connected topological group is nilpotent, because its fundamental group is abelian and acts trivially on the higher homotopy groups.
The torus $S^1\times S^1$ is nilpotent: its fundamental group $\mathbb{Z}^2$ is abelian, and its higher homotopy groups vanish.
Non-example: $\mathbb{R}P^2$ is not nilpotent, because $\pi_1=\mathbb{Z}/2$ acts on $\pi_2=\mathbb{Z}$ by $-1$, and this action is not nilpotent.

steps: Let $X$ be a [simply connected space](c:simply-connected-space), so $\pi_1(X)$ is trivial.
The trivial group is nilpotent, and it acts trivially on every $\pi_n(X)$.
A trivial action is nilpotent: take the chain $\pi_n(X)\supseteq0$.
So $X$ is a nilpotent space.
links.why: It shows that nilpotent spaces extend simply connected spaces by some spaces with nontrivial $\pi_1$.

reminder: The nine-point circle of a [triangle](c:triangle) passes through nine points: three side midpoints, three altitude feet, and three orthocenter-to-vertex midpoints.
definition: The nine-point circle of a [triangle](c:triangle) $ABC$ is the [circle](c:circle) through the three [midpoints](c:midpoint) of its sides. It also passes through the three feet of the altitudes and through the midpoints of $HA$, $HB$ and $HC$, where $H$ is the orthocenter. Its center is the midpoint of $OH$ for the circumcenter $O$, and its radius is half the circumradius.
examples: In the right triangle with legs $3$ and $4$, the circumradius is $5/2$, so the nine-point circle has radius $5/4$.
In an equilateral triangle the altitude feet are the side midpoints, so the nine points give only six distinct points on the circle.
Non-example: the circumcircle of a triangle is not its nine-point circle, because its radius is $R$, twice the radius of the nine-point circle.

reminder: A function is non-differentiable at a point when its difference quotient has no finite limit there.
definition: A function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is non-differentiable at a point $a$ when the [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) $\lim_{h\to0}(f(a+h)-f(a))/h$ does not exist as a real number, so $f$ has no [derivative](c:derivative) at $a$. This happens at a jump, at a corner, at a vertical tangent, and where the quotient oscillates.
examples: The function $|x|$ is non-differentiable at $0$, because the one-sided quotients tend to $-1$ and $1$.
The function $x\sin(1/x)$ with value $0$ at $0$ is non-differentiable at $0$, because the quotient $\sin(1/h)$ oscillates.
The Weierstrass function is continuous everywhere and non-differentiable at every point.
Non-example: $x^2$ is a [differentiable function](c:differentiable-function) with derivative $2x$, so it has no point of non-differentiability.

reminder: A Hopf subalgebra is normal when the adjoint action of the whole [Hopf algebra](c:hopf-algebra) keeps it inside itself.
definition: Let $H$ be a [Hopf algebra](c:hopf-algebra) with coproduct $\Delta(h)=\sum h_{(1)}\otimes h_{(2)}$ and antipode $S$. A Hopf subalgebra $K$ of $H$ is normal when $\sum h_{(1)}kS(h_{(2)})\in K$ and $\sum S(h_{(1)})kh_{(2)}\in K$ for all $h\in H$ and $k\in K$. These two conditions say that $K$ is stable under the left and right adjoint actions of $H$.
examples: For a group $G$ and a field $k$, the Hopf subalgebra $k[N]$ of the group algebra $k[G]$ is normal exactly when $N$ is a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) of $G$.
Every Hopf algebra $H$ is a normal Hopf subalgebra of itself, and so is the subalgebra $k\cdot1$.
Non-example: in $k[S_3]$ the Hopf subalgebra $k[\langle(1\,2)\rangle]$ is not normal, because $\langle(1\,2)\rangle$ is not a normal subgroup of $S_3$.

steps: Take a group $G$ and its group algebra $k[G]$, a [Hopf algebra](c:hopf-algebra) with $\Delta(g)=g\otimes g$ and $S(g)=g^{-1}$.
For $h=g$ the adjoint action sends $n\in N$ to $gng^{-1}$.
So $k[N]$ is stable under the adjoint action exactly when $gNg^{-1}\subseteq N$ for all $g\in G$.
That is the condition that $N$ is a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) of $G$.
links.why: It shows that a normal Hopf subalgebra extends the normal subgroup of a group to Hopf algebras.

reminder: A [subring](c:subring) of a [division ring](c:division-ring) is normal when conjugation by every nonzero element keeps it inside itself.
definition: A [subring](c:subring) $S$ of a [division ring](c:division-ring) $D$ is normal when $xsx^{-1}\in S$ for all $s\in S$ and all nonzero $x\in D$. Equivalently, $S$ is stable under every [inner automorphism](c:inner-automorphism) of $D$.
examples: The center of a division ring $D$ is a normal subring, because $xzx^{-1}=z$ for every central $z$.
The prime subfield of $D$ is a normal subring, because it lies in the center.
Non-example: in the quaternions $\mathbb{H}$ the subfield $\mathbb{C}=\mathbb{R}+\mathbb{R}i$ is not normal, because $(1+j)\,i\,(1+j)^{-1}=-k$ is not in $\mathbb{C}$.

steps: A normal subring $S$ of $D$ is first of all a [subring](c:subring) of $D$.
Add the condition that $xSx^{-1}\subseteq S$ for every nonzero $x\in D$.
A subring that meets this condition is a normal subring.
links.why: It shows that normality is an extra condition on a subring: invariance under conjugation, as for a normal subgroup.

reminder: Null infinity is the null part of the conformal boundary of a spacetime, where outgoing light rays end and incoming ones begin.
definition: In the [conformal compactification](c:conformal-compactification) of an [asymptotically flat spacetime](c:asymptotically-flat-spacetime), null infinity is the pair of null hypersurfaces $\mathscr{I}^+$ and $\mathscr{I}^-$ that form part of the boundary. Future null infinity $\mathscr{I}^+$ is where outgoing light rays end, and past null infinity $\mathscr{I}^-$ is where incoming light rays begin.
examples: In [Minkowski space](c:minkowski-space) every outgoing null geodesic ends on $\mathscr{I}^+$, a null hypersurface of topology $\mathbb{R}\times S^2$.
In the exterior of a Schwarzschild black hole, the conformal compactification has the same kind of null boundary $\mathscr{I}^\pm$, with topology $\mathbb{R}\times S^2$.
Non-example: spatial infinity $i^0$ and future timelike infinity $i^+$ are single boundary points, so they are not part of null infinity.

reminder: The right Ore condition says that $rs'=sr'$ has a solution with $s'\in S$ for all $r\in R$ and $s\in S$.
definition: Let $R$ be a [ring](c:ring) and let $S\subseteq R$ be a [multiplicative subset](c:multiplicative-subset) of elements that are not [zero-divisors](c:zero-divisor). The set $S$ satisfies the right Ore condition when for all $r\in R$ and $s\in S$ there are $r'\in R$ and $s'\in S$ with $rs'=sr'$. Then every left fraction $s^{-1}r$ equals a right fraction $r's'^{-1}$, and the [localization](c:localization-of-a-ring) of $R$ at $S$ exists as a ring of fractions.
examples: Every commutative ring satisfies the Ore condition for every multiplicative set, because $rs=sr$ gives $r'=r$ and $s'=s$.
Every right Noetherian domain satisfies the right Ore condition for its nonzero elements, for example the first Weyl algebra over $\mathbb{Q}$.
Non-example: in the free algebra $k\langle x,y\rangle$ with $S$ the nonzero elements, $xs'=yr'$ has no solution with $s'\ne0$, so the Ore condition fails.

steps: Let $R$ be a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) and $S$ a multiplicative set of non-zero-divisors.
Given $r\in R$ and $s\in S$, take $s'=s$ and $r'=r$.
Then $rs'=rs=sr=sr'$ because $R$ is commutative.
So $S$ satisfies the Ore condition, and commutativity makes the condition automatic.
links.why: It shows that the Ore condition is what lets a noncommutative ring have fractions, as a commutative ring does.

reminder: An orthomodular [lattice](c:lattice) has an orthocomplement and obeys the law that $x\le y$ implies $y=x\vee(x'\wedge y)$.
definition: An orthomodular lattice is a [lattice](c:lattice) $L$ with least element $0$, greatest element $1$ and a map $x\mapsto x'$ such that $x''=x$, $x\le y$ implies $y'\le x'$, $x\vee x'=1$ and $x\wedge x'=0$. In addition, $x\le y$ must imply $y=x\vee(x'\wedge y)$; this orthomodular law is a weak form of [modularity](c:is-modular-lattice).
examples: Every [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) is an orthomodular lattice, with the complement as orthocomplement.
The lattice of closed subspaces of a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) is an orthomodular lattice, with $M'=M^\perp$.
Non-example: the hexagon with chains $0<x<y<1$ and $0<y'<x'<1$ is an orthocomplemented lattice but not orthomodular, because $x\le y$ and $x\vee(x'\wedge y)=x\ne y$.

steps: Let $B$ be a [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) and take its complement as the orthocomplement $x\mapsto x'$.
This map has $x''=x$, reverses order, and satisfies $x\vee x'=1$ and $x\wedge x'=0$.
If $x\le y$, distributivity gives $x\vee(x'\wedge y)=(x\vee x')\wedge(x\vee y)=1\wedge y=y$.
So $B$ is an orthomodular lattice, and the Boolean case adds distributivity.
links.why: It shows that orthomodular lattices extend Boolean algebras by dropping distributivity.

steps: The closed subspaces of a Hilbert space form a lattice $L$ with $M\wedge N=M\cap N$ and $M'=M^\perp$.
This lattice satisfies the orthomodular law, so $L$ is an orthomodular lattice.
A [Hilbert lattice](c:hilbert-lattice) is an orthomodular lattice that also meets further conditions, such as completeness and the covering law.
links.why: It shows that a Hilbert lattice is an orthomodular lattice with extra conditions that match closed subspaces of a Hilbert space.

steps: Let $L$ be an orthomodular lattice with orthocomplement $x\mapsto x'$.
Each $x'$ satisfies $x\vee x'=1$ and $x\wedge x'=0$, so $x'$ is a complement of $x$.
So $L$ is a [complemented lattice](c:complemented-lattice), and the orthomodular case chooses the complements to form an orthocomplement obeying the orthomodular law.
links.why: It shows that the orthocomplement is a canonical choice of complements, and that the orthomodular law restricts how they behave.

reminder: A $p$-adic representation is a continuous linear action of a [topological group](c:topological-group) on a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{Q}_p$.
definition: Let $G$ be a [topological group](c:topological-group) and $V$ a finite-dimensional [vector space](c:vector-space) over the field $\mathbb{Q}_p$ of [p-adic numbers](c:p-adic-number). A $p$-adic representation of $G$ on $V$ is a [group representation](c:group-representation) $G\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ that is continuous for the $p$-adic topology. In number theory $G$ is usually a [Galois group](c:galois-group), and the scalars may form a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}_p$.
examples: The $p$-adic cyclotomic character $\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})\to\mathbb{Z}_p^\times\subset\mathrm{GL}_1(\mathbb{Q}_p)$ is a one-dimensional $p$-adic representation.
The $p$-adic Tate module of an elliptic curve $E$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, tensored with $\mathbb{Q}_p$, is a two-dimensional $p$-adic representation of $\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$.

Non-example: the regular representation of $\mathbb{Z}_p$ on the space of locally constant functions $\mathbb{Z}_p\to\mathbb{Q}_p$ has infinite dimension, so it is not a $p$-adic representation in this sense.

steps: A [group representation](c:group-representation) is a group $G$ acting linearly on a vector space $V$.
Choose $G$ a topological group and $V$ a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{Q}_p$.
Require that the map $G\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ is continuous for the $p$-adic topology.
The result is a $p$-adic representation.
links.why: It shows that direct sums, duals and tensor products of group representations carry over, as long as continuity is kept.

reminder: A packing of a region is a family of shapes inside it with pairwise disjoint interiors.
definition: A packing of a set $C$, the container, is a family of [subsets](c:subset) of $C$ whose [interiors](c:interior) are pairwise [disjoint](c:disjoint-subsets). The pieces may touch along their boundaries, but they may not overlap, and they need not cover $C$.
examples: Unit discs placed in a square without overlap form a packing of the square.
Dominoes of size $1\times2$ laid on a chessboard without overlap form a packing, and a packing that covers the board is a tiling.
Non-example: two unit discs whose centers are at distance $1$ do not form a packing, because their interiors intersect.

steps: Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a [tessellation](c:tesselation), a family of tiles that cover the plane with no overlaps.
The tiles of $\mathcal{T}$ have pairwise disjoint interiors, so $\mathcal{T}$ is a packing of the plane.
The tessellation adds the condition that the tiles leave no gaps.
links.why: It shows that a tessellation is a packing with no gaps.

reminder: A pencil of rational curves is a one-parameter family of curves on a surface whose general member is rational.
definition: A pencil on an [algebraic surface](c:algebraic-surface) $S$ is a one-parameter family $\{C_t\}_{t\in\mathbb{P}^1}$ of curves, the fibers of a rational map $S\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^1$ to the [projective line](c:projective-line). It is a pencil of rational curves when the general member $C_t$ is rational, that is, [birational](c:birational-map) to the projective line.
examples: The lines through a fixed point of $\mathbb{P}^2$ form a pencil of rational curves, and each line is isomorphic to $\mathbb{P}^1$.
On $\mathbb{P}^1\times\mathbb{P}^1$ the fibers of the first projection form a pencil of rational curves.
The conics through four general points of $\mathbb{P}^2$ form a pencil of rational curves.
Non-example: a general pencil of plane cubics has smooth cubics as general members, and these have genus $1$, so they are not rational.

reminder: A [subgroup](c:subgroup) is perfect when it equals its own commutator subgroup.
definition: A [subgroup](c:subgroup) $H$ of a [group](c:group) $G$ is perfect when $[H,H]=H$, where $[H,H]$ is the [commutator subgroup](c:commutator-subgroup) of $H$. Equivalently, every element of $H$ is a product of commutators of elements of $H$.
examples: The trivial subgroup is perfect, and so is the alternating group $A_5$ as a subgroup of $S_5$.
The group $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ is a perfect subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$.
Non-example: a nontrivial abelian subgroup is not perfect, because its commutator subgroup is trivial.

steps: Let $G$ be a [perfect group](c:is-perfect), so $[G,G]=G$.
Take $H=G$ as a subgroup of $G$.
Then $[H,H]=H$, so $G$ is a perfect subgroup of itself.
links.why: It shows that a perfect group is the case $H=G$ of a perfect subgroup.

reminder: A [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral) has perpendicular diagonals when its two diagonals meet at a right angle.
definition: A [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral) $ABCD$ has perpendicular diagonals when the lines $AC$ and $BD$ are [perpendicular](c:perpendicular), that is, $\overrightarrow{AC}\cdot\overrightarrow{BD}=0$. Equivalently, $AB^2+CD^2=BC^2+DA^2$.
examples: A [square](c:square) and, more generally, a rhombus have perpendicular diagonals.
A kite has perpendicular diagonals.
Non-example: a rectangle that is not a square does not have perpendicular diagonals, because its equal diagonals cross at an angle other than $90^\circ$.

reminder: A dissection of a polygon cuts it into finitely many polygons with disjoint interiors that together fill it.
definition: A dissection of a [polygon](c:polygon) $P$ is a finite family of polygons $P_1,\dots,P_k$ whose [union](c:union) is $P$ and whose [interiors](c:interior) are pairwise disjoint. The pieces may share boundary segments, but they leave no gaps and no overlaps.
examples: A diagonal of a convex quadrilateral cuts it into two triangles, which is a dissection into two pieces.
A $2\times3$ rectangle is dissected into six unit squares.
Non-example: two overlapping triangles that cover a quadrilateral do not form a dissection, because their interiors intersect.

steps: Let $T$ be a [polygon triangulation](c:polygon-triangulation) of $P$, so $P$ is the union of the triangles of $T$.
The triangles of $T$ do not overlap, so their interiors are pairwise disjoint.
Hence $T$ is a dissection of $P$ whose pieces are all triangles.
links.why: It shows that a triangulation is a dissection with triangles as pieces, so results on dissections apply to it.

reminder: The poset of commutative subalgebras of an algebra $A$ is the set of its commutative subalgebras ordered by inclusion.
definition: For an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) $A$ that need not be [commutative](c:commutative-algebra), the poset $\mathrm{ComSub}(A)$ is the set of all commutative [subalgebras](c:subalgebra) $B\subseteq A$, with the [partial order](c:partial-order) given by inclusion. The presheaf topos on this poset is the [Bohr topos](c:bohr-topos) of $A$.
examples: If $A$ is commutative, then $\mathrm{ComSub}(A)$ has a greatest element, namely $A$ itself.
For $A=M_2(\mathbb{C})$ the scalar matrices form the least unital element, and every maximal element has dimension $2$.
Non-example: $M_2(\mathbb{C})$ itself is not an element of $\mathrm{ComSub}(M_2(\mathbb{C}))$, because it is not commutative.

reminder: A predicate is a statement with variables that becomes true or false when each variable gets a value.
definition: A predicate on a [set](c:set) $X$ is a statement $P(x)$ about a [variable](c:variable) $x$ that becomes a [proposition](c:proposition), true or false, once a value from $X$ replaces $x$. Equivalently, it is a [function](c:function) from $X$ to the truth values. A predicate in $n$ variables is defined in the same way on $X_1\times\dots\times X_n$.
examples: The statement ‘$x$ is even’ is a predicate on $\mathbb{Z}$, true at $4$ and false at $5$.
The statement $x<y$ is a predicate in two variables on $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}$.
Non-example: the expression $x^2+1$ is not a predicate, because it gives a number and not a truth value.

steps: Let $p$ be a [proposition](c:proposition), a statement that is true or false.
View $p$ as a predicate in zero variables.
It has no variable to replace, so its value is the fixed truth value of $p$.
So a proposition is a predicate without variables.
links.why: It shows that a predicate is a proposition with open slots for values.

reminder: A pretopos is a category with finite limits that is both Barr-exact and [extensive](c:extensive-category).
definition: A pretopos is a [regular category](c:regular-category) in which every equivalence relation is a kernel pair, which is Barr-exactness, and which is [extensive](c:extensive-category): finite coproducts exist, are disjoint, and are stable under pullback. It follows that a pretopos is a [coherent category](c:coherent-category).
examples: The category of sets is a pretopos, and so is the category of finite sets.
Every [Grothendieck topos](c:grothendieck-topos) is a pretopos.
Non-example: the category of abelian groups is exact but not extensive, because its finite coproduct is the product, so coproducts are not disjoint.

steps: A pretopos is a [regular category](c:regular-category), so it has finite limits and stable images.
It has stable finite coproducts, and the union of two subobjects is the image of their coproduct.
So finite unions of subobjects exist and are stable under pullback.
Hence a pretopos is a [coherent category](c:coherent-category), and the pretopos case adds exactness and disjoint coproducts.
links.why: It shows that coherent logic has an interpretation in every pretopos.

steps: Let $\mathcal{E}$ be a [Grothendieck topos](c:grothendieck-topos), a category of sheaves on a site.
It has finite limits, and every equivalence relation in it is a kernel pair.
Its coproducts are disjoint and stable under pullback, so it is extensive.
So $\mathcal{E}$ is a pretopos, and the Grothendieck case adds a small generating set and all small colimits.
links.why: It shows that a pretopos keeps the exactness properties of a topos and drops the size and colimit conditions.

reminder: A primitive group is a transitive [permutation group](c:permutation-group) that preserves no partition of the set except the trivial ones.
definition: A [permutation group](c:permutation-group) $G$ on a set $X$ with $|X|\ge2$ is primitive when it is [transitive](c:is-pretransitive) and preserves only two partitions of $X$: the partition into singletons and the partition with one block. Equivalently, $G$ is transitive and a point stabilizer is a maximal subgroup of $G$.
examples: The groups $S_n$ and $A_n$ acting on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ are primitive for $n\ge3$.
A cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/p$ of prime order $p$ acting on itself is primitive, because no block has a size between $1$ and $p$.
Non-example: the dihedral group $D_4$ acting on the four vertices of a square is not primitive, because the two pairs of opposite vertices form an invariant partition.

steps: A primitive group acts [transitively](c:is-pretransitive) on $X$ by definition.
Add the condition that the only invariant partitions of $X$ are the trivial ones.
A transitive action with this extra condition is primitive.
links.why: It shows that primitivity is transitivity plus the absence of nontrivial blocks.

reminder: A primitive set of integers is a set in which no element divides another.
definition: A set $A$ of [natural numbers](c:natural-number) greater than $1$ is primitive when no element of $A$ [divides](c:divisibility) another element of $A$. That is, $a\mid b$ with $a,b\in A$ implies $a=b$.
examples: The set of all prime numbers is primitive.
The set of integers in the interval $(n,2n]$ is primitive, because a proper multiple of $a>n$ is at least $2a>2n$.
The set of integers with exactly $k$ prime factors, counted with multiplicity, is primitive.
Non-example: $\{2,3,6\}$ is not primitive, because $2$ divides $6$.

steps: Order the integers greater than $1$ by divisibility, with $a\le b$ when $a\mid b$; this is a [partial order](c:partial-order).
Two elements $a,b$ are incomparable when neither divides the other.
An [antichain](c:antichain) is a set of pairwise incomparable elements.
So a set is primitive exactly when it is an antichain for divisibility.
links.why: It shows that primitive sets are antichains of the divisibility order, so facts about antichains apply to them.

reminder: A quadratic irrational is an irrational real number that is a root of a quadratic polynomial with integer coefficients.
definition:
A [real number](c:real-number) $\alpha$ is a quadratic irrational when it is [irrational](c:irrational-number) and satisfies $a\alpha^2+b\alpha+c=0$ for some [integers](c:integer) $a,b,c$ with $a
e0$. Equivalently, $\alpha=(p+q\sqrt d)/r$ for integers $p,q,r$ with $q
e0$ and $r
e0$ and a squarefree integer $d>1$.
examples: The numbers $\sqrt2$ and the golden ratio $(1+\sqrt5)/2$ are quadratic irrationals.
A real number with an eventually periodic continued fraction is a quadratic irrational.
Non-example: $\sqrt[3]{2}$ is irrational but not a quadratic irrational, because its [minimal polynomial](c:minimal-polynomial) $x^3-2$ has degree $3$.
Non-example: $1/2$ is a root of $2x-1$, but it is rational, so it is not a quadratic irrational.

steps: A quadratic irrational $\alpha$ is a root of a nonzero integer polynomial of degree $2$.
So $\alpha$ is an [algebraic number](c:algebraic-number).
Because $\alpha$ is irrational, its minimal polynomial has degree exactly $2$.
So the quadratic irrationals are the real algebraic numbers of degree $2$.
links.why: It places the quadratic irrationals among the algebraic numbers as those of degree $2$.

reminder: The quadratrix is the curve traced by the meeting point of a uniformly moving line and a uniformly turning radius.
definition: A horizontal line moves at constant speed from the $x$-axis up to the line $y=1$. In the same time, a radius of the unit [circle](c:circle) about the origin turns at constant speed from the $x$-axis to the $y$-axis. The quadratrix is the [curve](c:curve) traced by the meeting point of the line and the radius; it has the equation $x=y\cot(\pi y/2)$ for $0<y\le1$.
examples: The curve ends at $(0,1)$ on the line $y=1$, and it tends to the point $(2/\pi,0)$ on the $x$-axis as $y\to0$.
The quadratrix trisects any [angle](c:angle) up to $90^\circ$: the angle is $\pi y/2$ at height $y$, so the point at one third of the height has one third of the angle.
Non-example: the Archimedean spiral also combines two uniform motions, but it is not the quadratrix, because a point moves along the turning radius instead of a line moving across.

reminder: A reflection fixes a [hyperplane](c:hyperplane) pointwise and sends each vector orthogonal to it to its negative.
definition: A reflection of an [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) $V$ is a [linear map](c:linear-map) $r$ that fixes a [hyperplane](c:hyperplane) $H$ pointwise and sends each vector orthogonal to $H$ to its negative. For a nonzero vector $a$, the reflection in $H=a^\perp$ is $r_a(x)=x-2\frac{\langle x,a\rangle}{\langle a,a\rangle}a$. In a Euclidean space, the same description with an affine hyperplane gives an affine reflection.
examples: In $\mathbb{R}^2$ the reflection in the $x$-axis is the map $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$.
In $\mathbb{R}^3$ the reflection in the plane $z=0$ is the map $(x,y,z)\mapsto(x,y,-z)$.
Non-example: the rotation by $180^\circ$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is not a reflection, because it fixes only the origin and no line.

steps: Write $r_a(x)=x-c_xa$ with $c_x=2\langle x,a\rangle/\langle a,a\rangle$.
Expand $\langle r_a(x),r_a(y)\rangle$; the three correction terms add up to zero.
So $r_a$ is linear and preserves the inner product.
Hence every reflection is an [orthogonal transformation](c:orthogonal-transformation) with determinant $-1$.
links.why: It shows that reflections are the simplest orthogonal transformations, the generators in the Cartan–Dieudonné theorem.

steps: Every vector of $V$ is a sum $h+ta$ with $h\in H$ and $a$ orthogonal to $H$.
A reflection $r$ fixes $h$ and sends $ta$ to $-ta$, so $r(r(x))=x$ for every $x$.
So $r$ is an [involution](c:involution), a map that is its own inverse.
links.why: It shows that applying a reflection twice gives the identity.

reminder: A regulated function on an interval has a left limit and a right limit at every point.
definition: A function $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ is regulated when it has one-sided [limits](c:limit-of-a-function) $f(x^-)$ and $f(x^+)$ at every point, where only the existing side counts at $a$ and $b$. Equivalently, $f$ is the [uniform limit](c:uniform-convergence) of [step functions](c:step-function).
examples: Every continuous function on $[a,b]$ is regulated.
Every [monotone function](c:monotone-function) on $[a,b]$ is regulated, and so is every function of bounded variation.
The sign function is regulated: at $0$ its one-sided limits are $-1$ and $1$.
Non-example: the function $\sin(1/x)$ on $[0,1]$ with value $0$ at $0$ is not regulated, because its right limit at $0$ does not exist.

steps: Let $f$ be a [continuous function](c:continuous-function) on $[a,b]$.
At each point $x$ the one-sided limits exist and equal $f(x)$.
So $f$ is regulated.
Regulated functions also allow jump discontinuities.
links.why: It shows that regulated functions extend continuous functions by allowing jumps.

steps: Let $f$ be a [function of bounded variation](c:bounded-variation) on $[a,b]$.
By the Jordan decomposition, $f=g-h$ with $g$ and $h$ increasing.
An increasing function has one-sided limits at every point.
So $f=g-h$ has them too, and $f$ is regulated.
links.why: It shows that results for regulated functions cover every function of bounded variation.

reminder: A repeating decimal has a decimal expansion whose digits end in a block that repeats forever.
definition: A repeating decimal is a [real number](c:real-number) whose decimal expansion is eventually periodic: from some digit on, a fixed finite block of digits repeats forever. These numbers are exactly the [rational numbers](c:rational-number).
examples: The numbers $1/3=0.\overline{3}$ and $1/7=0.\overline{142857}$ are repeating decimals.
The number $1/6=0.1\overline{6}$ repeats after a first digit that is not part of the block.
A terminating decimal such as $0.25$ repeats the block $0$ forever.
Non-example: $\sqrt2=1.41421356\ldots$ has no repeating block, so it is not a repeating decimal.

reminder: A Riesz space is a real vector space with a compatible order in which every two elements have a supremum and an infimum.
definition: A Riesz space, or vector lattice, is a real [vector space](c:vector-space) $E$ with a partial order such that $x\le y$ implies $x+a\le y+a$ for all $a$ and $tx\le ty$ for all $t\ge0$. In addition, $E$ is a [lattice](c:lattice): every pair $x,y$ has a least upper bound $x\vee y$ and a greatest lower bound $x\wedge y$.
examples: The space $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the coordinatewise order is a Riesz space, and $x\vee y$ is the coordinatewise maximum.
The space of continuous real functions on $[0,1]$ with the pointwise order is a Riesz space, with $(f\vee g)(t)=\max(f(t),g(t))$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{R}^3$ ordered by the cone $z\ge\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ is an ordered vector space but not a lattice, so it is not a Riesz space.

steps: Let $E$ be a Riesz space with order $\le$.
By definition every pair $x,y\in E$ has a join and a meet for this order.
So $(E,\le)$ is a [lattice](c:lattice) once the vector space structure is forgotten.
The Riesz case adds a real vector space structure that is compatible with the order.
links.why: It shows that every Riesz space is a lattice, so lattice results apply to it.

steps: Let $E$ be a [Banach lattice](c:banach-lattice), a Banach space with an order that makes it a vector lattice.
Its order is compatible with the vector space structure and has all pairwise suprema and infima.
So $E$ is a Riesz space.
The Banach case adds a complete norm that respects the lattice order.
links.why: It shows that facts proved for Riesz spaces also hold in every Banach lattice.

reminder: A circular sector of radius $r$ and angle $\theta$ in radians has area $\frac12r^2\theta$.
definition: A circular sector of radius $r$ and central [angle](c:angle) $\theta$, measured in radians, is the part of a disc of radius $r$ between two radii at angle $\theta$. Its [area](c:area) is $\frac12r^2\theta$, which is the fraction $\theta/2\pi$ of the [area enclosed by a circle](c:area-enclosed-by-a-circle) $\pi r^2$.
examples: A quarter of a disc of radius $2$ has $\theta=\pi/2$ and area $\frac12\cdot4\cdot\frac\pi2=\pi$.
A sector of radius $3$ and angle $60^\circ=\pi/3$ has area $\frac12\cdot9\cdot\frac\pi3=\frac{3\pi}{2}$.
Non-example: if the angle is in degrees, the formula $\frac12r^2\theta$ gives a wrong area; for $\theta=90$ it gives $45r^2$ instead of $\frac\pi4r^2$.

steps: Take the full angle $\theta=2\pi$, so the sector is the whole disc.
The formula gives $\frac12r^2\cdot2\pi=\pi r^2$.
This is the [area enclosed by a circle](c:area-enclosed-by-a-circle).
links.why: It shows that the area $\pi r^2$ of a disc is the case of a full angle.

reminder: A semilinear set is a finite union of sets $b+\mathbb{N}p_1+\dots+\mathbb{N}p_k$ in $\mathbb{N}^d$.
definition: A subset of $\mathbb{N}^d$ is linear when it has the form $\{b+n_1p_1+\dots+n_kp_k:n_i\in\mathbb{N}\}$ for a base vector $b$ and period vectors $p_1,\dots,p_k$ in $\mathbb{N}^d$. A subset is semilinear when it is a finite [union](c:union) of linear sets. For $d=1$ these are the ultimately periodic subsets of $\mathbb{N}$.
examples: The set of even numbers is a linear subset of $\mathbb{N}$, with $b=0$ and period $p_1=2$.
The set $\{(m,n):m\le n\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}^2$ is linear, with $b=(0,0)$ and periods $(1,1)$ and $(0,1)$.
Every finite subset of $\mathbb{N}^d$ is semilinear, as a union of linear sets with no periods.
Non-example: the set of squares $\{n^2:n\in\mathbb{N}\}$ is not semilinear, because it is not ultimately periodic.

reminder: An [algebraic extension](c:algebraic-extension) is separable when every element has a minimal polynomial with distinct roots.
definition: A [polynomial](c:polynomial) over a [field](c:field) $K$ is separable when all its irreducible factors have distinct roots in the [algebraic closure](c:algebraic-closure) $\bar K$. An [algebraic extension](c:algebraic-extension) $L/K$ is separable when the [minimal polynomial](c:minimal-polynomial) over $K$ of every element of $L$ is separable.
examples: Every algebraic extension of $\mathbb{Q}$, such as $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)/\mathbb{Q}$, is separable, because the characteristic is $0$.
Every algebraic extension of a finite field, such as $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}/\mathbb{F}_p$, is separable.
Non-example: $\mathbb{F}_p(t)/\mathbb{F}_p(t^p)$ is not separable, because the minimal polynomial $x^p-t^p=(x-t)^p$ of $t$ has only one root.

steps: Let $L/K$ be a [Galois extension](c:galois-extension), which is algebraic, normal and separable.
In particular each element of $L$ has a separable minimal polynomial over $K$.
So $L/K$ is a separable extension.
The Galois case adds normality: the minimal polynomials split completely in $L$.
links.why: It shows that separability is half of the Galois condition, together with normality.

steps: A separable extension is first of all an [algebraic extension](c:algebraic-extension).
Add the condition that each minimal polynomial has distinct roots.
An algebraic extension with this condition is separable.
links.why: It shows that separability is one extra condition on the minimal polynomials of an algebraic extension.

reminder: A sequential [colimit](c:colimit) is the colimit of a chain of maps $X_0\to X_1\to X_2\to\cdots$.
definition: A sequential colimit is the [colimit](c:colimit) of a diagram $X_0\xrightarrow{f_0}X_1\xrightarrow{f_1}X_2\xrightarrow{f_2}\cdots$ indexed by the [natural numbers](c:natural-number). It is an object $X_\infty$ with maps $i_n:X_n\to X_\infty$ such that $i_{n+1}f_n=i_n$, and it is universal with this property.
examples: In sets, an increasing union $A_0\subseteq A_1\subseteq\cdots$ is the sequential colimit of the inclusions.
The space $\mathbb{C}P^\infty$ is the sequential colimit of $\mathbb{C}P^0\subset\mathbb{C}P^1\subset\mathbb{C}P^2\subset\cdots$ in topological spaces.
The sequence $\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{2}\cdots$ has the colimit $\mathbb{Z}[1/2]$ in abelian groups.
Non-example: a pushout is the colimit of a span $X\leftarrow Z\to Y$, whose index category is not the natural numbers, so it is not a sequential colimit.

steps: Order the natural numbers by $\le$; this is a directed poset.
A sequence $X_0\to X_1\to\cdots$ is a diagram on this poset.
Its colimit is therefore a [directed colimit](c:directed-colimit).
The sequential case uses the single directed set $\mathbb{N}$.
links.why: It shows that results about directed colimits apply to sequential colimits.

steps: A sequence $X_0\to X_1\to\cdots$ is a diagram in a category.
A [colimit](c:colimit) of this diagram is a universal cocone under it.
So a sequential colimit is a colimit whose index category is $\mathbb{N}$.
links.why: It shows that a sequential colimit has the universal property of every colimit.

reminder: A $\sigma$-ideal is a family of subsets closed under subsets and countable unions.
definition: A $\sigma$-ideal on a [set](c:set) $X$ is a family $\mathcal{I}$ of subsets of $X$ that contains the [empty set](c:empty-set) and every [subset](c:subset) of each of its members. It also contains the [union](c:union) of every [countable](c:countable-set) family of its members. It is proper when $X\notin\mathcal{I}$.
examples: The Lebesgue null sets of $\mathbb{R}$ form a proper $\sigma$-ideal.
The countable subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ form a $\sigma$-ideal, and so do the meager subsets of $\mathbb{R}$.
Non-example: the finite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ do not form a $\sigma$-ideal, because the countable union $\bigcup_n\{n\}=\mathbb{N}$ of members is not finite.

steps: Order the [power set](c:power-set) $\mathcal{P}(X)$ by inclusion, so it is a lattice with unions as joins.
A $\sigma$-ideal $\mathcal{I}$ is nonempty and closed under subsets, so it is a lower set.
It is closed under the union of two members, so it is directed.
So $\mathcal{I}$ is an [order ideal](c:is-ideal) that is also closed under countable unions.
links.why: It shows that a $\sigma$-ideal is an order ideal of the power set with closure under countable unions added.

reminder: A star-polycategory is a [polycategory](c:polycategory) in which every object has a dual.
definition: A [polycategory](c:polycategory) has objects and morphisms $\Gamma\to\Delta$ between finite lists of objects, composed by cutting along one object. It is a star-polycategory when every object $A$ has a dual $A^*$, so that morphisms $\Gamma,A\to\Delta$ correspond naturally to morphisms $\Gamma\to A^*,\Delta$.
examples: Finite-dimensional vector spaces, with morphisms $A_1,\dots,A_m\to B_1,\dots,B_n$ the linear maps $A_1\otimes\cdots\otimes A_m\to B_1\otimes\cdots\otimes B_n$, form a star-polycategory with $A^*$ the dual space.
A model of classical linear logic with negation as its only connective is a star-polycategory.

Non-example: a multicategory with an object, seen as a polycategory with single outputs, is not a star-polycategory. A dual $A^*$ would turn the identity of $A^*$ into a morphism $A^*,A\to{}$ with no output.

steps: A star-polycategory is first of all a [polycategory](c:polycategory).
Add a dual $A^*$ for every object $A$, with a natural bijection between $\Gamma,A\to\Delta$ and $\Gamma\to A^*,\Delta$.
A polycategory with this extra structure is a star-polycategory.
links.why: It shows that a star-polycategory is a polycategory with duals for all objects.

steps: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a [star-autonomous category](c:star-autonomous-category) with a tensor product and a par.
Keep the objects of $\mathcal{C}$, and let a morphism $\Gamma\to\Delta$ be a map from the tensor of $\Gamma$ to the par of $\Delta$.
The duality $A^*$ of $\mathcal{C}$ gives the bijection between $\Gamma,A\to\Delta$ and $\Gamma\to A^*,\Delta$.
So $\mathcal{C}$ gives a star-polycategory, and a star-autonomous category is the representable special case.
links.why: It shows that star-polycategories are to star-autonomous categories what multicategories are to monoidal categories.

reminder: A submonoid is a subset that contains the unit and is closed under the product.
definition: A submonoid of a [monoid](c:monoid) $M$ with unit $1$ is a [subset](c:subset) $N\subseteq M$ with $1\in N$ and $xy\in N$ for all $x,y\in N$. Then $N$ is itself a monoid for the inherited product.
examples: The even numbers form a submonoid of $(\mathbb{Z},+)$, and so do the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$.
The set $\{1,2,4,8,\dots\}$ of powers of $2$ is a submonoid of $(\mathbb{Z},\cdot)$.
Non-example: the odd numbers are not a submonoid of $(\mathbb{Z},+)$, because $0$ is not odd and $1+1=2$ is not odd.

steps: Let $H$ be a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of a group $G$, where $G$ is a monoid.
By definition $H$ contains the identity element and is closed under products.
So $H$ is a submonoid of $G$.
The subgroup case adds that $H$ is also closed under inverses.
links.why: It shows that a subgroup is a submonoid that also contains inverses.

steps: Let $S$ be a [multiplicative subset](c:multiplicative-subset) of a ring $R$, so $1\in S$ and $S$ is closed under multiplication.
The ring $R$ is a monoid under multiplication.
So $S$ is a submonoid of $(R,\cdot)$.
Many authors add the condition $0\notin S$ for a multiplicative subset.
links.why: It shows that a multiplicative subset is a submonoid of the multiplicative monoid of a ring.

reminder: A sum-free set contains no solution of $x+y=z$ with $x$, $y$ and $z$ all in the set.
definition: A subset $A$ of the [integers](c:integer), or of an [abelian group](c:abelian-group), is sum-free when there are no $x,y,z\in A$ with $x+y=z$, where $x$ and $y$ may be equal. Equivalently, $(A+A)\cap A=\emptyset$.
examples: The odd integers are sum-free, because the sum of two odd integers is even.
The set $\{n+1,\dots,2n+1\}$ is sum-free, because any sum of two of its elements is at least $2n+2$.
The integers congruent to $1$ or $4$ modulo $5$ form a sum-free set, because $1+1$, $1+4$ and $4+4$ are $2$, $0$ and $3$ modulo $5$.
Non-example: $\{1,2,3\}$ is not sum-free, because $1+1=2$ and $1+2=3$.

reminder: The superpotential is a holomorphic function of the chiral superfields that sets the non-gauge interactions of a supersymmetric theory.
definition: In a four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=1$ [supersymmetric](c:supersymmetry) field theory, the superpotential $W(\Phi^i)$ is a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) of the chiral [superfields](c:superspace) $\Phi^i$ only, and not of their conjugates. It enters the [action](c:action-functional) through the term $\int d^4x\,d^2\theta\,W+\text{h.c.}$, and it gives the scalar potential $V=\sum_i|\partial W/\partial\phi^i|^2$ and the Yukawa couplings $\frac12\,\partial_i\partial_jW\,\psi^i\psi^j$.
examples: The Wess–Zumino model has $W=\frac12m\Phi^2+\frac13\lambda\Phi^3$, which gives the potential $V=|m\phi+\lambda\phi^2|^2$.
A free massless chiral multiplet has $W=0$, so it has no scalar potential.
Non-example: the term $\bar\Phi\Phi$ is not a superpotential, because it depends on the conjugate field; it belongs to the Kähler potential.

reminder: A symmetric monoidal infinity-groupoid is an infinity-groupoid with a product that is associative and commutative up to coherent homotopy.
definition: A symmetric monoidal infinity-groupoid is an [infinity-groupoid](c:infinity-groupoid) $X$ with a unit and a product $X\times X\to X$ that is associative, unital and commutative up to coherent higher homotopies. Equivalently, it is a [symmetric monoidal (infinity,1)-category](c:symmetric-monoidal-infinity-1-category) in which every morphism is invertible, and it is the same as an [E-infinity space](c:e-infinity-space).
examples: A commutative monoid, viewed as a discrete infinity-groupoid, is a symmetric monoidal infinity-groupoid.
The groupoid of finite sets and bijections, with disjoint union as the product, is a symmetric monoidal infinity-groupoid.
Every infinite loop space, such as the space $\mathbb{Z}\times BU$, is a symmetric monoidal infinity-groupoid.
Non-example: the category of sets with the cartesian product is a symmetric monoidal category, but not an infinity-groupoid, because it has morphisms that are not invertible.

steps: Let $X$ be a symmetric monoidal infinity-groupoid, viewed as an (infinity,1)-category.
Its product is associative, unital and commutative up to coherent homotopy.
So $X$ is a [symmetric monoidal (infinity,1)-category](c:symmetric-monoidal-infinity-1-category).
The groupoid case adds that every morphism is invertible.
links.why: It shows that results on symmetric monoidal (infinity,1)-categories apply to symmetric monoidal infinity-groupoids.

steps: Let $A$ be an [abelian group](c:abelian-group).
View $A$ as a discrete infinity-groupoid, with only identity higher morphisms.
The group law is associative and commutative on the nose, so all coherence homotopies are identities.
So $A$ is a symmetric monoidal infinity-groupoid, and the general case lets the laws hold only up to homotopy.
links.why: It shows that symmetric monoidal infinity-groupoids extend abelian groups by letting the laws hold up to homotopy.

reminder: T-duality is an equivalence between the quantum theories of two different [sigma-model](c:sigma-model) targets, such as circles of radius $R$ and $1/R$.
definition: T-duality is a relation between two [sigma-models](c:sigma-model) with different targets whose quantum theories, such as [conformal field theories](c:conformal-field-theory), are equivalent. For circle targets of radius $R$ and $1/R$ in string units, it exchanges momentum modes with winding modes. In topological T-duality, a [circle bundle](c:circle-bundle) $E\to B$ with flux $H$ is dual to a circle bundle $\hat E\to B$ with flux $\hat H$, and each Chern class is the fiber integral of the other flux.
examples: A closed string on a circle of radius $R$ is T-dual to a closed string on a circle of radius $1/R$ in string units.
The 3-sphere $S^3$ as the Hopf bundle over $S^2$ with flux $k$ is T-dual to the lens space $S^3/\mathbb{Z}_k$ with flux $1$.
Non-example: a rotation of the target circle gives an isomorphic sigma-model, not a T-dual one, because the radius does not change.

reminder: A [topological space](c:topological-space) is $T_1$ when every singleton set is closed.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is $T_1$ when $\{x\}$ is a [closed set](c:closed-set) for every $x\in X$. Equivalently, for any two points $x\ne y$ there is an [open set](c:open-set) that contains $x$ and not $y$.
examples: Every [metric space](c:metric-space) is $T_1$, and so is every [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space).
The real line with the cofinite topology is $T_1$ but not Hausdorff.
Non-example: the Sierpiński space $\{0,1\}$ with open sets $\emptyset$, $\{1\}$ and $\{0,1\}$ is not $T_1$, because $\{1\}$ is not closed.

steps: Let $X$ be a [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space) and fix $x\in X$.
For each $y\ne x$ choose an open set $V_y$ that contains $y$ and misses $x$.
The union of all $V_y$ is $X\setminus\{x\}$, so $X\setminus\{x\}$ is open.
So $\{x\}$ is closed for every $x$, and $X$ is $T_1$.
links.why: It shows that $T_1$ is the weaker condition: Hausdorff spaces separate points by disjoint open sets, and $T_1$ spaces only need single points to be closed.

steps: Let $X$ be a $T_1$ space and let $x\ne y$ in $X$.
The set $X\setminus\{y\}$ is open and contains $x$ but not $y$.
So some open set separates $x$ from $y$, which is the Kolmogorov condition.
The $T_1$ case asks for such a set in both directions.
links.why: It shows that $T_1$ strengthens the Kolmogorov condition from one-sided to two-sided separation of points.

reminder: A tagged [prepartition](c:prepartition) of a box is a prepartition with one chosen tag point for each box.
definition: Let $I$ be a [box](c:box) in $\mathbb{R}^n$. A [prepartition](c:prepartition) of $I$ is a finite set of pairwise disjoint boxes contained in $I$. A tagged prepartition of $I$ is a prepartition together with a tag point $x_J$ in the closed box $I$ for each box $J$ of the prepartition.
examples: The boxes $(0,\frac12]$ and $(\frac12,1]$ with tags $\frac14$ and $\frac34$ form a tagged prepartition of $(0,1]$.
The single box $J=(0,\frac12]$ with tag $x_J=1$ is a tagged prepartition of $I=(0,1]$; it covers only part of $I$, and the tag lies outside $J$.
Non-example: the boxes $(0,\frac23]$ and $(\frac13,1]$ with any tags are not a tagged prepartition, because the boxes are not disjoint.

steps: Let $\pi$ be a [tagged partition](c:tagged-partition) of $I$, a tagged prepartition whose boxes cover $I$.
Its boxes are finitely many, pairwise disjoint, and contained in $I$.
Each box carries a tag point in $I$.
So $\pi$ is a tagged prepartition, and the partition case adds that the boxes cover $I$.
links.why: It shows that the tagged partitions used in Riemann sums are the tagged prepartitions whose boxes cover the whole box.

reminder: A terminal object $1$ of a [category](c:category) receives exactly one morphism from every object.
definition: An [object](c:object) $1$ of a [category](c:category) $\mathcal{C}$ is terminal when, for every object $X$ of $\mathcal{C}$, there is exactly one morphism $X\to1$. Any two terminal objects are [isomorphic](c:isomorphism) by a unique isomorphism.
examples: In the category of sets, every one-element set is terminal.
In a poset seen as a category, the terminal object is the greatest element.
In the category of groups, the trivial group is terminal, and it is also initial.
Non-example: the empty set is not terminal in the category of sets, because there is no function from a nonempty set into it.

steps: Take the empty diagram in $\mathcal{C}$.
A cone over the empty diagram is just an object $X$ of $\mathcal{C}$.
A [limit](c:limit-category-theory) is a universal cone, so it is an object $L$ with a unique morphism from every $X$.
That is a terminal object, so the terminal object is the limit of the empty diagram.
links.why: It shows that a terminal object is the limit of the empty diagram.

steps: Let $0$ be a [zero object](c:is-zero) of $\mathcal{C}$, which is both initial and terminal.
Then for every object $X$ there is exactly one morphism $X\to0$.
So $0$ is a terminal object.
The zero object adds that $0$ is also initial.
links.why: It shows that a zero object is a terminal object that is also initial.

reminder: Twisted cohomology is cohomology with coefficients in a [local system](c:local-system), or twisted by a class in higher cohomology.
definition: Let $L$ be a [local system](c:local-system) of abelian groups on a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$, that is, a locally constant family of groups with automorphisms around loops. The twisted cohomology $H^n(X;L)$ is the [cohomology](c:cohomology) of the cochain complex of $X$ with coefficients in $L$. More generally, a cohomology theory can be twisted by a class in a higher cohomology group.
examples: For the constant local system with value $\mathbb{Z}$, twisted cohomology is ordinary cohomology $H^n(X;\mathbb{Z})$.

On a closed manifold $M$ of dimension $n$, cohomology with the orientation local system $\mathbb{Z}^w$ satisfies Poincaré duality $H^k(M;\mathbb{Z}^w)\cong H_{n-k}(M;\mathbb{Z})$, even if $M$ is not orientable.
[Twisted K-theory](c:twisted-k-theory) is K-theory twisted by a class in $H^3(X;\mathbb{Z})$.
Non-example: cohomology with coefficients in a skyscraper sheaf at a point is sheaf cohomology, but the sheaf is not locally constant, so it is not twisted cohomology in this sense.

steps: Let $A$ be an abelian group and let $L$ be the constant local system with value $A$.
A constant local system has trivial monodromy around every loop.
Cohomology with coefficients in $L$ is then ordinary [cohomology](c:cohomology) $H^n(X;A)$.
So twisted cohomology contains ordinary cohomology as the case of a trivial twist.
links.why: It shows that twisted cohomology extends ordinary cohomology by letting the coefficients change around loops.

reminder: Twisted K-theory is K-theory twisted by a degree-3 cohomology class, such as a [Dixmier-Douady class](c:dixmier-douady-class).
definition: Let $X$ be a space and $H\in H^3(X;\mathbb{Z})$ a class. Choose a [principal bundle](c:principal-bundle) $P$ with structure group $PU(\mathcal{H})$ whose [Dixmier-Douady class](c:dixmier-douady-class) is $H$, and let $\mathrm{Fred}(P)$ be the associated bundle of [Fredholm operators](c:fredholm-operator). The twisted K-theory $K^0(X,H)$ is the group of homotopy classes of sections of $\mathrm{Fred}(P)$, and it is [topological K-theory](c:topological-k-theory) when $H=0$.
examples: For $H=0$ twisted K-theory is ordinary topological K-theory.
For the 3-sphere $S^3$ and $H=k$ times a generator, $K^0(S^3,H)=0$ and $K^1(S^3,H)\cong\mathbb{Z}/k$.
Non-example: a complex line bundle on $X$, with class in $H^2(X;\mathbb{Z})$, gives no twist, because tensoring with it is an isomorphism of ordinary K-theory.

steps: Take the twist $H=0$, so $P$ is the trivial $PU(\mathcal{H})$-bundle.
The associated bundle of Fredholm operators is $X\times\mathrm{Fred}$.
Its sections are maps $X\to\mathrm{Fred}$, so $K^0(X,0)$ is the group $[X,\mathrm{Fred}]$.
By the Atiyah–Jänich theorem this group is the [topological K-theory](c:topological-k-theory) $K^0(X)$.
links.why: It shows that twisted K-theory extends ordinary K-theory, which is the case of zero twist.

steps: Twisted cohomology allows a cohomology theory $E$ to be twisted by a class.
Take $E$ to be K-theory, whose twists include the classes in $H^3(X;\mathbb{Z})$.
The $E$-cohomology twisted by such a class is twisted K-theory.
links.why: It shows that twisted K-theory is one case of twisted cohomology, so general facts on twisted cohomology apply.

reminder: An ultracategory is a [category](c:category) with coherent ultraproduct functors for all [ultrafilters](c:ultrafilter).
definition: An ultracategory is a [category](c:category) $\mathcal{C}$ with, for every set $X$ and every [ultrafilter](c:ultrafilter) $\mu$ on $X$, an ultraproduct functor $\int_\mu:\mathcal{C}^X\to\mathcal{C}$. Coherent isomorphisms make these functors compatible with composition of ultrafilters. The standard example is the category of models of a coherent theory, with the ordinary [ultraproduct](c:ultraproduct) of models.
examples: The category of sets is an ultracategory, and $\int_\mu A_x$ is the ordinary ultraproduct of the sets $A_x$.
The category of models of a coherent theory is an ultracategory, with the ultraproduct of models as $\int_\mu$.
Non-example: a category with no chosen ultraproduct functors is not an ultracategory, because the ultraproducts are extra structure and not a property.

reminder: The ultrafilter extension of a [Kripke frame](c:kripke-frame) is a new frame whose points are the ultrafilters of the old one.
definition: Let $F=(W,R)$ be a [Kripke frame](c:kripke-frame). Its ultrafilter extension $\mathrm{ue}(F)$ has as points the [ultrafilters](c:ultrafilter) $u$ on $W$, with $u\,R^{ue}\,v$ when $\{w\in W:\exists x\in X,\ wRx\}\in u$ for every $X\in v$.
examples: For a finite frame $F$ every ultrafilter is principal, so $\mathrm{ue}(F)$ is isomorphic to $F$.
For $(\mathbb{N},\le)$ the extension has the non-principal ultrafilters as extra points, and every ultrafilter sees every non-principal ultrafilter.
Non-example: for an infinite frame $F$, the frame $F$ itself is not $\mathrm{ue}(F)$, because $\mathrm{ue}(F)$ also has non-principal ultrafilters as points.

reminder: A vector is an element of a [vector space](c:vector-space); in the plane or in space it has a magnitude and a direction.
definition: A vector is an [element](c:element) of a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over a field, so vectors can be added and multiplied by scalars. In the plane or in space, a vector is a displacement with a length and a direction, drawn as an arrow. Two arrows with the same length and direction are the same vector.
examples: In $\mathbb{R}^2$ the pair $(3,4)$ is a vector of length $5$.
A polynomial of degree at most $2$ is a vector in the space of such polynomials.
The velocity of a moving point is a tangent vector.
Non-example: a temperature such as $20$ degrees is a scalar and not a vector, because it has no direction.

reminder: A voting system turns the voters' rankings of the alternatives into a set of winning alternatives.
definition: A voting system for a finite set $A$ of alternatives and $n$ voters is a [function](c:function) that assigns a nonempty set of winning alternatives to every profile $(\succ_1,\dots,\succ_n)$. Each $\succ_i$ is a strict ranking of $A$, that is, a [total order](c:total-order). If the winner is always a single alternative, the system is a [social choice function](c:social-choice-function).
examples: Plurality voting makes each voter vote for the top-ranked alternative, and the alternatives with the most votes win.
A dictatorship lets one fixed voter decide, and the winner is the top-ranked alternative of that voter.
Non-example: a rule that outputs a full ranking of $A$ is a [social welfare function](c:social-welfare-function), not a voting system, because its output is not a set of winners.

steps: Let $f$ be a [social choice function](c:social-choice-function) that maps each profile to one alternative.
Replace each winner $f(P)$ by the singleton set $\{f(P)\}$.
This set is nonempty, so the new rule is a voting system.
The single-winner case adds that every winning set has exactly one element.
links.why: It shows that results about voting systems also hold for social choice functions.

reminder: A Walrasian equilibrium is a price vector and an allocation in which each agent gets a best affordable bundle and the markets clear.
definition: Consider an exchange economy with agents $i=1,\dots,m$. Agent $i$ has an endowment $e_i\in\mathbb{R}^k_{\ge0}$ in [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) and a [preference relation](c:preference-relation) $\succsim_i$ on bundles. A Walrasian equilibrium is a price vector $p$ and an allocation $(x_i)$ such that each $x_i$ is $\succsim_i$-best in the budget set $\{x\ge0:p\cdot x\le p\cdot e_i\}$ and $\sum_ix_i=\sum_ie_i$.
examples: Two agents with utility $u(x,y)=xy$ and endowments $e_1=(1,0)$ and $e_2=(0,1)$ have the Walrasian equilibrium $p=(1,1)$ with $x_1=x_2=(\frac12,\frac12)$.
One agent with utility $u(x,y)=\min(x,y)$ and endowment $e=(1,1)$ has the Walrasian equilibrium $p=(1,1)$ with $x=e$.

Non-example: in the economy of the first example, $p=(2,1)$ is not an equilibrium price vector. The demands total $\frac34$ of the first good and $\frac32$ of the second, but the supply is $1$ of each.

reminder: A 2-Segal space is a simplicial space whose simplices on a polygon are determined by any triangulation of that polygon.
definition: A 2-Segal space is a [simplicial object](c:simplicial-object) $X$ in spaces such that, for every [triangulation](c:polygon-triangulation) $T$ of the $(n+1)$-gon, the map $X_n\to X_T$ is an equivalence. Here $X_T$ glues one copy of $X_2$ for each triangle of $T$ along the interior edges by [homotopy pullbacks](c:homotopy-pullback). In particular, for the two triangulations of a square, the maps $X_3\to X_2\times^h_{X_1}X_2$ are equivalences.
examples: The nerve of a category is a 2-Segal simplicial set, because a chain of composable morphisms determines the composites on every triangulation.
The Waldhausen S-construction of an exact category is a 2-Segal space.
Non-example: the simplicial set generated by two 2-simplices $(0,1,2)$ and $(0,2,3)$ glued along the edge $(0,2)$, with no 3-simplex, is not 2-Segal, because the glued pair has no 3-simplex over it.

steps: Let $X$ be a [Segal space](c:segal-space), so $X_n$ is equivalent to the iterated fiber product $X_1\times^h_{X_0}\cdots\times^h_{X_0}X_1$.
A triangle of $X$ is then a pair of composable edges together with their composite.
Gluing triangles along edges records a chain of composable edges, so $X_T\simeq X_n$ for each triangulation $T$.
So $X$ is a 2-Segal space, and the Segal case has a unique composite for each pair of edges.
links.why: It shows that 2-Segal spaces extend categories and Segal spaces by allowing composition to be multivalued.

reminder: The 2-sphere $S^2$ is the set of points at distance $1$ from the origin in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
definition: The 2-sphere is $S^2=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3:x^2+y^2+z^2=1\}$ with the subspace topology from [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb{R}^3$. It is the [sphere](c:sphere) of dimension $2$, and stereographic projection makes it homeomorphic to the [Riemann sphere](c:riemann-sphere) $\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}$.
examples: The surface of a ball in space is a 2-sphere.
The one-point compactification of the plane is a 2-sphere.
Non-example: the torus $S^1\times S^1$ is a closed surface but not a 2-sphere, because it is not simply connected.

steps: The $n$-[sphere](c:sphere) is $S^n=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}:\|x\|=1\}$.
Choose $n=2$ in this definition.
Then $S^2=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^3:\|x\|=1\}$ is the 2-sphere.
links.why: It shows that every fact about $n$-spheres holds for the 2-sphere.
